sections.heading: Resetting a password you still know
sections.text:
You can change your NSID password at any time from the self-service password page. Sign in with your current password, then choose a new one. Changes take effect immediately, but devices that have the old password saved will keep prompting until you update them.

After changing your password you will need to update it anywhere it is stored: the wireless network on your phone and laptop, any mail app configured manually, and any mapped network drives.

sections.heading: Resetting a password you have forgotten
sections.text:
If you cannot sign in, use the forgotten password option on the sign-in page. You will be asked to verify your identity using the recovery method registered on your account, which is usually a personal email address or a phone number.

If no recovery method is registered, or you no longer have access to it, self-service reset will not work. In that case contact the service desk, who will verify your identity before resetting the account.

sections.heading: Password requirements
sections.text:
Passwords must meet a minimum length and complexity requirement, and cannot reuse a recent previous password. Passphrases of several words are easier to remember and generally stronger than short complex strings.

Passwords expire on a set schedule. You will receive reminder notices by email before expiry. If a password expires while you are away, the forgotten password process still applies.

sections.heading: Why accounts lock
sections.text:
Accounts lock automatically after several failed sign-in attempts. The most common cause is not a forgotten password but a device still holding an old one and retrying in the background, which locks the account repeatedly even after a successful reset elsewhere.

If your account locks again within minutes of being unlocked, a saved password on one of your devices is almost always the cause.

sections.heading: Clearing a lockout
sections.text:
A lockout clears automatically after a set period. You do not need to contact anyone unless it recurs.

Before signing in again, update the saved password on every device: wireless network settings, mail applications, and any service where you chose to stay signed in. Signing out of all sessions and back in resolves most repeat lockouts.

sections.heading: Registering your first method
sections.text:
Multi-factor authentication requires a second confirmation when you sign in. The recommended method is an authenticator app on your phone, which generates a code or sends a push notification. A phone number for text or voice can be registered as a backup.

Register at least two methods. Accounts with only one registered method are the most common reason people lose access when they change phones.

sections.heading: Getting a new phone
sections.text:
Register your new device before disposing of the old one. Sign in using the existing method, then add the new device as an additional method and remove the old one.

If you have already lost access to every registered method, self-service will not work and the service desk must verify your identity before resetting your MFA registration.

sections.heading: When prompts do not arrive
sections.text:
Push notifications require the phone to have an internet connection. If prompts do not appear, open the authenticator app directly and use the code it displays rather than waiting for a notification.

Codes are time-based, so a phone whose clock has drifted will generate codes that are rejected. Enabling automatic date and time on the device resolves this.

sections.heading: Signing in to eduroam
sections.text:
Select the eduroam network and sign in with your full username including the institution suffix, not your username alone. This is the single most common cause of a connection being rejected.

The first connection on each device may ask you to accept a certificate. Accept it only if the certificate details match those published in this article.

sections.heading: Using eduroam elsewhere
sections.text:
Eduroam works at participating institutions worldwide using the same credentials. You do not need to register anything before travelling.

If it fails at another institution but works on campus, the usual cause is a saved profile from a previous visit. Removing the network and adding it again resolves most cases.

sections.heading: When the connection keeps dropping
sections.text:
Repeated disconnections shortly after a password change mean the device is still presenting the old credentials. Remove the saved network entirely and reconnect with the new password.

Older devices that support only outdated wireless standards may connect intermittently in busy areas. The guest network is a fallback for these, although it does not provide access to internal services.

sections.heading: When you need the VPN
sections.text:
Most services, including email and the learning management system, work from anywhere without a VPN. The VPN is required only for resources restricted to the campus network, such as some library databases, internal administrative systems and certain research file shares.

If a service works on campus but not at home, that is the signal you need the VPN.

sections.heading: Installing and connecting
sections.text:
Download the client from the software page and sign in with your usual credentials. Multi-factor authentication applies to VPN sign-in as well.

Connect only while you need the restricted resource. Leaving the VPN connected routes unnecessary traffic through the campus network and can slow other activity.

sections.heading: Setting up email on a phone
sections.text:
Add the account using the built-in mail application and choose the organisational account option rather than manual server setup. Automatic configuration retrieves the correct settings and applies any required security policies.

Manual setup with server names is not supported and will usually fail authentication once multi-factor authentication is enforced.

sections.heading: Mail that will not send or receive
sections.text:
A mailbox that has reached its storage limit will continue receiving but stop sending. Check your mailbox size before troubleshooting anything else. Emptying deleted items and the junk folder recovers space immediately.

If messages sit in the outbox on one device but send correctly from the web, the saved password on that device is likely out of date.

sections.heading: Missing messages
sections.text:
Check the junk folder and any rules you have created before reporting a message as missing. Rules created years ago are a frequent cause of mail appearing to vanish.

Messages deleted from deleted items can be recovered for a limited period using the recover deleted items option in the web client.

sections.heading: A course is missing from your list
sections.text:
Courses appear only after the instructor publishes them, which often happens on or shortly before the first day of class. A registered course that does not appear is usually unpublished rather than misassigned.

If the course is published and other students can see it but you cannot, the issue is with your registration rather than with the system, and the registration office handles that.

sections.heading: Uploads and submissions failing
sections.text:
Uploads fail most often because of file size limits or an unsupported file type. Check the size limit stated on the assignment before troubleshooting the connection.

Submitting from a phone on a weak connection is the second most common cause. Where possible, submit from a computer on a stable connection, and confirm the submission receipt before closing the page.

sections.heading: Content that will not display
sections.text:
Embedded video and interactive content can be blocked by browser privacy settings or extensions. Trying the same page in a private window with extensions disabled identifies this quickly.

Clearing the browser cache resolves most display problems that persist after an instructor updates content.

sections.heading: Sending a job to a campus printer
sections.text:
Print jobs are sent to a shared queue and released at any campus printer by signing in at the device. Jobs waiting in the queue are deleted automatically after a set period, so release them the same day.

Printing from a personal laptop requires the print client to be installed, or you can upload the file through the web print page instead.

sections.heading: Print credit
sections.text:
Printing is charged against a print balance linked to your account. The balance can be topped up online and is shown when you sign in at a device.

A job that disappears without printing usually means the balance was too low to cover it. The job is not held; it must be sent again after topping up.

sections.heading: Quality and jams
sections.text:
Report a jam or a fault using the number posted on the device rather than attempting to clear it yourself.

Pages printing faint or streaked indicate a toner problem, which is also reported rather than fixed locally.

sections.heading: What is available
sections.text:
Students have access to the standard office suite, several statistical and mathematical packages, and reference management software at no additional cost while enrolled. Availability differs by program, and some titles are licensed only for teaching use.

Install these from the software portal rather than from a vendor site, so the correct licence is applied automatically.

sections.heading: Licences after you leave
sections.text:
Licences tied to enrolment stop working after you graduate or withdraw. Files created with the software remain yours, but the applications will require a personal licence to continue using.

Export anything stored only inside a licensed application before your access ends.

sections.heading: Activation failures
sections.text:
A title that installs but will not activate is usually signed in with a personal account rather than the institutional one. Sign out completely and sign back in with your full institutional username.

Some licences allow a limited number of simultaneous installations. Deactivating an old device frees a slot.

sections.heading: First steps on a new laptop
sections.text:
Connect to the wireless network, sign in to your institutional account in a browser, then install the office suite and the print client from the software portal.

Register the device with multi-factor authentication before you need it urgently. Doing this while you still have access to your existing method avoids the most common lockout.

sections.heading: Moving from an old device
sections.text:
Files stored in the institutional cloud storage appear automatically once you sign in. Files stored only on the old device must be copied across manually before it is wiped.

Saved wireless passwords and mail accounts do not transfer. Expect to set those up again.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.text:
Messages that create urgency about your account, ask you to confirm a password, or link to a sign-in page from an unfamiliar address should be treated as suspicious. Legitimate messages about your account will not ask you to enter your password by following a link in an email.

Job and scholarship offers that arrive unsolicited and ask for payment or bank details are a recurring pattern targeting students.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.text:
Do not reply, do not follow links, and do not open attachments. Report the message using the reporting option in your mail client, which sends it for analysis.

If you have already entered your password on a suspicious page, change it immediately and then contact the service desk. Speed matters more than certainty here.

sections.heading: How to open a ticket
sections.text:
Requests can be submitted through the online support portal, by email, or in person at the service desk. The portal is the fastest route because it captures the information needed to start work without a follow-up exchange.

Include what you were trying to do, what happened instead, the exact wording of any error message, and which device and browser you were using.

sections.heading: What the desk cannot do by email
sections.text:
Anything that grants or restores access requires identity verification, so password resets, multi-factor authentication resets and account unlocks cannot be completed by email alone.

Bring photo identification if you attend in person, or expect to verify your identity another way if you contact the desk remotely.

sections.heading: Hours and response times
sections.text:
The desk operates during published business hours, with reduced hours between terms and on holidays. Tickets submitted outside those hours are queued for the next working day.

Urgent issues affecting teaching or an exam should be flagged as such when the ticket is created.
